D011_m001.question:
It’s been about eight months now—maybe longer—that I just haven’t been able to quiet my mind. I’m constantly running through scenarios: deals falling apart, clients pulling out, something going wrong with my presentations. Even when I’m off the clock, it’s like my brain won’t shut down. I’ll be brushing my teeth or driving to the airport, and suddenly I’m caught in this loop about a minor email I sent last week—what if it was misinterpreted? My chest tightens, and I can’t focus on anything else.  

I used to thrive under pressure—deadlines, late-night negotiations—but now I feel like I’m always on edge. I can’t sit still. My leg bounces during meetings, and I’ve started pacing in hotel rooms. My back’s been killing me, and my shoulders are so tight I can barely turn my head some mornings. My arms and legs feel heavy, like I’ve been sprinting for hours, even when I haven’t moved.  

I thought it was just stress at first—the travel, the divorce, the workload. But it’s not going away. I’m exhausted, but my body won’t relax. Even when nothing’s wrong, I feel like something’s about to go wrong.
D011_m001.options:
A. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Specific Phobia

D011_m002.question:

I’ll be grading papers and suddenly start worrying about my rent, then my students’ performance, then whether my car needs repairs, then if my mom’s doing okay. It’s not like one problem—it’s everything, all at once, and it just never stops.

These worries pop up out of nowhere, even in the middle of class. I’ll be explaining an equation and catch myself thinking, “What if I mess up the lesson? What if I get fired? What if I never meet someone, never settle down?” I can’t focus—my mind races and I feel stuck in it.

Physically, it’s like I’m always braced for something bad. My shoulders are so tight, and the back of my neck is one solid knot. Some days, it turns into a headache that won’t quit. I try to relax after school, but I just can’t—I sit on the couch, stiff as a board, like I’m still holding my breath, waiting for something to go wrong.

    D. Specific Phobia
